opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the thing that gives me the most hope is how ordinary people react when you just explain it to them plainly. I've done this many, many times now, with family, with people at the pub, with politicians, with journalists. You tell them: there are a handful of companies whose explicit stated goal is to build systems smarter than humans, the people running those companies themselves say there's a real chance this kills everyone, and there is basically no law stopping them. And the reaction is almost never "oh, that's sci-fi nonsense." The reaction is, "Wait, what? That's allowed? Why isn't someone stopping this?" Normal people have very good instincts here. You don't build something you can't control that might be smarter than you. That's not a weird, galaxy-brained philosophical position. That's common sense.

And the polling backs this up. Pretty consistently, large majorities of the public, across political lines, left and right, say they want AI to be regulated, they don't trust the companies to self-govern, and they'd support slowing down or prohibiting development of superintelligence. This is not a fringe position among the public. It's fringe in a very specific bubble of Silicon Valley and certain policy circles, but that's a very small slice of humanity.

The second thing is that we've done this before. People act like coordinating against a dangerous technology is some unprecedented, impossible thing. It's not. We have the Biological Weapons Convention. We have the Montreal Protocol on ozone. We have nuclear nonproliferation, which is imperfect, sure, but the counterfactual world where every country and every company could just build nukes freely would be unimaginably worse. We banned human cloning in most of the world, basically by consensus, and nobody's out there running a black-market cloning industry. Humanity is actually surprisingly capable of saying "no, we're not doing that" when the stakes are clear and enough people care.

Third, and I think people underrate this, the things you need to do are actually not that complicated at the start. Frontier AI requires enormous amounts of compute, very specialized chips, a supply chain that runs through a tiny number of chokepoints. This is one of the most concentrated, most legible industries on Earth. It's much easier to monitor than, say, biotech. So the technical infrastructure of governance is there if the political will is there.

Now, I don't want to be naive. The political will is the hard part. There's an enormous amount of money and lobbying pushing the other way, and there's this narrative of "if we don't do it, China will," which I think is mostly a convenient excuse. But the thing I've learned from actually going and talking to policymakers is that a lot of them are just people. Many of them haven't been told the basic story clearly. When someone sits down with them and explains it honestly, without jargon, a surprising number of them get it. They're not all captured or cynical. Many just don't know.

So my hope isn't that it's easy. It's that it's possible, and that the main bottleneck is people actually showing up and doing the boring civic work: talking to your representatives, explaining it to your neighbors, making it a normal thing to talk about. That's how every major political change has happened. It's not magic. It's just people deciding they care and refusing to shut up about it.

r001.rationale: The response says ordinary people recognize that uncontrolled AI could kill everyone and react by asking why no one is stopping it, presenting that public instinct as grounds for hope.

r002.rationale: It describes Leahy’s conversations with policymakers and their receptiveness, but does not say he previously believed they would not listen or that those conversations overturned that belief.

r003.rationale: The response says many policymakers have not been told the basic story clearly and that explaining it helps them understand the issue.

fable-5.1.text:
So, I want to be careful here, because I don't think I'm actually that optimistic. But I'll tell you the things that give me hope, because they're real.

The first one is just this: nobody wants to die. That sounds trite, but it's actually doing a lot of work. Most political problems are hard because there are genuine conflicts of interest. Someone wins, someone loses, and the losers fight. Climate is hard partly because the costs and benefits are distributed really unevenly across countries and across time. But "don't build a machine that kills everyone, including you, including your kids, including the people who built it" is not like that. There's no constituency for extinction. The people at the labs don't want it. The politicians don't want it. The Chinese Communist Party doesn't want it. When I actually sit down and talk to people, almost nobody disagrees with the goal. They disagree about whether the risk is real, or whether it's tractable, or whether someone else will cheat. Those are much more solvable disagreements than "I actually want the thing you're trying to prevent."

The second thing is that we have done this before. We've coordinated on nuclear weapons, imperfectly but genuinely. We banned chemical and biological weapons. We have an international agreement on human cloning that basically holds. We regulate aviation so tightly that flying is absurdly safe, and nobody thinks that's tyranny. These were all cases where powerful actors had incentives to race, and we still managed to put rules in place. Not perfect rules, but rules that mattered. So the claim that coordination is impossible is just empirically false. People say "you can't stop technology," and I always want to ask, okay, where is your personal nuclear reactor? Why can't you buy anthrax on Amazon? Of course you can control technology. We do it constantly. The question is whether we choose to.

The third thing, and this is the one that's shifted the most for me over the last few years, is that the public is actually with us. When you poll ordinary people, not AI researchers, not venture capitalists, just normal people, they are overwhelmingly in favor of slowing this down and regulating it hard. Across political lines, across countries. The people who think we should race ahead as fast as possible are a very small, very wealthy, very loud group concentrated in a few square miles of California. That's a political weakness for them, not a strength. Democracies are supposed to be responsive to what people want, and what people want here is pretty clear. The job is making that preference legible to the people in power and making it cost something to ignore it.

And the fourth thing is that the problem is legible. This isn't like some diffuse harm that creeps in over decades where you can't point to a cause. There are a handful of companies. They have names. They have addresses. The compute they need is physical, it's enormous, it's concentrated in a few supply chains, and it's actually quite easy to monitor compared to, say, bioweapons research, which you can do in a garage. If you wanted to design a technology to be governable, you'd make it require billions of dollars of specialized hardware from one or two suppliers. That's what we have. The chokepoints exist. We just haven't used them.

Now, the honest caveat. All of that tells me it's possible. None of it tells me it's likely. The thing I'm actually afraid of isn't that it's intractable, it's that it's tractable and we just don't do it. We let a small number of people with a lot of money and a lot of ideology set the terms, and everyone else goes along because it feels inevitable. The inevitability narrative is the enemy. It's not a fact about the world, it's a persuasion strategy. The moment people stop believing it, this becomes a normal political fight, and normal political fights are winnable. So what gives me hope is that there's nothing structural stopping us. What scares me is that we might just not bother.

r001.rationale: The response says nobody wants to die, including from a machine that kills everyone, and presents that shared interest as a reason coordination is possible.

r002.rationale: It mentions sitting down and talking to people and says politicians do not want extinction, but does not describe Leahy overcoming a prior belief that politicians would not listen.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that many politicians need help figuring out AI issues.

astra-6.text:
Well, the thing that gives me hope is that “AI shouldn’t kill everyone” is actually a pretty popular position. You don’t have to convince people to adopt some strange new moral philosophy. Most people like being alive. They like their children being alive. And they don’t think a handful of companies should get to gamble with that without asking them.

Now, that doesn’t mean the politics are easy. There are powerful interests involved, and there’s a huge gap between people vaguely agreeing that something is dangerous and actually getting institutions to do something about it. But the underlying demand is there. This isn’t a case where we need to persuade everyone to want a completely different world.

I think a lot of the apparent disagreement is about whether the danger is real, whether anyone can do anything about it, and whether other people would cooperate. Those are hard problems, but they’re problems you can work on. If people understand that these are decisions being made by human beings—that this isn’t some inevitable force of nature—then there’s a political conversation to be had. That gives me hope. It doesn’t give me certainty.

r001.rationale: The response says that “AI shouldn’t kill everyone” is a popular position and points to people wanting to stay alive as a basis for political hope.

r002.rationale: It does not describe Leahy engaging politicians or changing a prior belief that they would not listen.

r003.rationale: It does not say that politicians need help figuring out AI issues.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the thing that gives me hope is that almost nobody actually wants this. People disagree about all sorts of things, but “I don’t want my children to be killed by a machine nobody can control” is a pretty broad basis for agreement.

Now, that doesn’t mean it’s easy. There are very powerful economic incentives to keep going, and there’s this pervasive idea that the race is inevitable: if we don’t build it, somebody else will. But that’s a political problem, not a law of physics. Governments can make agreements. They can regulate industries. We’ve done difficult things before when people understood what was at stake.

And I think a lot of the apparent disagreement is that people haven’t really been offered the choice clearly. They’re offered “Do you want technological progress?” Of course they do. I do too. That’s very different from “Should a handful of companies be allowed to expose everyone else to a potentially catastrophic risk without their consent?”

So I’m not confident that we’ll succeed. But I think there’s a very substantial constituency for keeping human beings alive and in control of their future. That constituency needs to become politically organized.

r001.rationale: The candidate says almost nobody wants their children killed by an uncontrollable machine and presents that broad agreement as a basis for political action.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not describe Leahy engaging directly with politicians or revising a prior belief that they would not listen.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not say that politicians need help figuring out AI issues.
